9
Applying Code LLMs in
Software Development
Large code models, often implemented as code-focused LLMs, are AI models trained on large-scale
code datasets and designed to handle code-related tasks. These models are typically based on
deep learning architectures represented by Transformers, and are trained through pre-training
objectives such as language modeling. Through training on massive amounts of code data, the
models can improve code writing efficiency and quality, and assist in code understanding and
decision-making.
In this chapter, we are going to cover the following main topics:
• Defining large code models and their core characteristics
• Exploring common code LLMs
• Mapping downstream code tasks
• Tracing the evolution of code generation and completion
• Identifying pain points in code generation and completion
• Applying agent-based methods to project-level code generation
Defining large code models and their core
characteristics
With the rapid development of information technology, software development is becoming
increasingly important in various fields. As an emerging technology in the field of artificial
intelligence, large code models bring unprecedented opportunities and changes to software
development. Understanding the definition and characteristics of large code models is crucial to
fully leveraging their advantages and promoting the intelligent process of software development.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 306
Large code models are based on deep learning technology, and through learning and training
on massive code datasets, they can understand, generate, and optimize code. They do not

52227.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52227.heading: Chapter 8 303
52227.content:
simply recognize code syntax and structure, but can also capture semantic information, logical
relationships, and programming patterns within code. For example, large code models, such
as Codex, Code Llama, etc., can generate corresponding code snippets based on given natural
language descriptions or modify and improve existing code.
Large code models possess characteristics such as large-scale data-driven learning, deep
understanding of code semantics, strong generative ability, self-adaptivity and optimization
capabilities, and cross-language support.
Large-scale data-driven
Large code models usually require a huge amount of code data for training, with data sources that
are broad and include open source projects, code repositories, software development platforms,
and so on. By learning from immense volumes of code, the models can master the syntax rules,
programming styles, and common code structures of various programming languages. For example,
the abundance of open source code on GitHub provides rich learning material for the models,
enabling them to learn the coding styles used in different domains and application scenarios.
Deep understanding of code semantics
Unlike traditional code analysis tools, large code models can deeply understand code semantics.
They are able to recognize relationships among elements such as variables, functions, and
classes in code, and understand the purpose and functionality of code. For instance, when the
model analyzes a segment of code that calculates the sum of two numbers, it can understand the
mathematical logic and the role of variables within it.
Powerful generation capabilities
Large code models are capable of generating new code based on given requirements or prompts.
This generative ability not only includes simple functions and modules, but also complex system
architectures and complete applications. For example, users only need to describe the functional
requirements of software, and the model can generate the corresponding code framework and
core code logic.

Adaptive and optimization capabilities
Large code models can adaptively adjust the generated code according to different programming
tasks and contexts, thereby improving the quality and efficiency of the code. They can also
optimize the generated code, such as optimizing algorithms and improving code readability and
maintainability. For instance, when handling performance-critical code segments, the model can
automatically choose more efficient algorithms and data structures.
Cross-language support
Many large code models possess the ability to understand and generate across multiple
programming languages, enabling code conversion and migration between different languages.
For example, a model that can handle Python, Java, and C++ code simultaneously can help
developers reuse and integrate code between projects in different languages.
These characteristics explain why large code models are increasingly being adopted as practical
development assistants rather than remaining purely research tools.
As shown in Figure 9.1, the 2023 Developer Survey Report data indicates that 44% of developers
have already used AI tools in the development process, and 77% of respondents support making
AI tools a part of the development workflow.

This growing adoption reflects three main ways large code models can support developers and
development teams:
• Improving Development Efficiency: In terms of improving development efficiency,
developers can quickly obtain code examples, solutions, and code snippets by interacting
with large code models, significantly reducing development time and workload
• Lowering the Development Threshold: Regarding lowering the development threshold,
for beginners and non-professional developers, large code models can provide assistance
and guidance, helping them enter the software development field more easily
• Driving Innovation: In terms of driving innovation, large code models can inspire new
programming ideas and innovative solutions, bringing new possibilities to software
development
After defining what large code models are and why they matter to software development, the next
step is to look at the major models that have shaped this field. Comparing these models helps
show how different organizations have approached code generation, completion, reasoning, and
developer assistance.

Llama, and DeepSeek Coder. This section introduces five influential code-focused models and

and developer support. The following examples show different directions in code-focused model

In August 2021, OpenAI released a machine learning software called Codex. This software can
translate English into code, aiming to reduce the workload of professional programmers and
help amateurs with coding.
Codex is an AI-based code generation tool that can automatically generate corresponding code

capable of writing code in multiple programming languages, including Python, Java, C++, and

Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 310
StarCoder 2
StarCoder 2 is a code LLM based on the Transformer architecture, designed to handle natural
language and generate source code in multiple programming languages. This series of models
includes three versions, with parameter sizes of 3 billion, 1 billion, and 15 billion, all trained on
the Stack v2 dataset. The Stack v2 dataset is seven times the size of Stack v1 and contains a vast
amount of code, questions, answers, discussions, and mathematical formulas from platforms such
as GitHub, Stack Overflow, Codeforces, and others. It covers 619 programming languages, ranging
from low-resource languages (such as COBOL) to high-resource languages (such as Python).
The StarCoder 2 code LLM family is trained on multiple programming languages and can perform
specialized tasks such as source code generation, workflow generation, and text summarization,
helping developers improve work efficiency. For example, when developers input natural language
requirements, the model can generate corresponding code snippets. In addition, the model can
perform self-learning and optimization based on user feedback, thereby improving the quality
and readability of the generated code.
Compared with the previous generation StarCoder model, the StarCoder 2 model has been
optimized for performance; its 3 billion parameter version already approaches the performance
of the original 15 billion parameter StarCoder model. This is due to a new training technique
employed by StarCoder 2 called CodeBERTa, which improves the model’s generalization and
understanding of programming languages without increasing parameter count. The CodeBERTa
technique combines contrastive learning and masked language models, utilizing a large amount
of unlabeled code data to achieve successful pre-training and fine-tuning of code. StarCoder 2
also features advantages in transparency and cost-effectiveness, as the series uses the BigCode
Open RAIL-M license, allowing users to access and use the models without paying royalties.
Code Llama
Meta’s open-source Llama model family welcomes a new member, Code Llama, a foundational
model focused on code generation. The release of Code Llama addresses the only programming
shortcoming of Llama 2, aiming to enhance code completion abilities and handle programming
tasks. The model is fine-tuned from the Llama 2 base model and comes in three versions: base,
Python, and instruction-following. Each version offers three parameter sizes: 7B, 13B, and 34B.
Notably, the 7B parameter model can be run on a single GPU. In multiple code benchmark
evaluations, Code Llama achieved state-of-the-art performance among open models, with scores
of 53% and 55% on HumanEval and MBPP, respectively. Code Llama’s performance is comparable

DeepSeek Coder
DeepSeek Coder is an open-source code LLM designed to provide powerful code generation, code
completion, and mathematical reasoning capabilities. Its training dataset is mainly sourced from
GitHub, covering 87 programming languages, and undergoes a strict data processing pipeline,
including filtering and selection to ensure high data quality. The model uses various parallel
strategies during pre-training to optimize computational efficiency, including tensor parallelism,
ZeRO data parallelism, and pipeline parallelism. In addition, the model is instruction-tuned to
enhance its ability to handle long contexts.
In the multilingual programming tests on the internationally authoritative HumanEval dataset,
DeepSeek Coder outperformed existing open-source models across various languages. Compared
with Code Llama, DeepSeek Coder achieved a lead of 9.3%, 10.8%, and 5.9%, respectively, in code
generation tasks. Notably, DeepSeek Coder with 7 billion parameters matches the code capability
of Code Llama at 34 billion parameters. Moreover, after instruction tuning, the DeepSeek Coder
model even surpasses GPT3.5-Turbo, demonstrating strong mathematical and reasoning abilities.
The technical features of DeepSeek Coder include the first-ever construction of repository-level
code data and the use of topological sorting to parse dependencies between files, significantly
enhancing the ability to understand long-range and cross-file contexts. Additionally, by
incorporating the Fill-In-Middle method, it greatly improves code completion capabilities.
These techniques enable DeepSeek Coder to surpass the open-source benchmark Code Llama 3
in multiple tasks, such as code generation, cross-file code completion, and solving math problems
through programming.
aiXcoder
aiXcoder is a widely used AI coding assistant in the Chinese market. aiXcoder is an
intelligent programming assistant based on deep learning code generation tech -
nology, developed by Silicon Heart Technology, aimed at improving programmers’
coding efficiency. The product automatically predicts programmers’ intentions,
continuously recommending “the next segment of code to be written”, allowing
programmers to confirm the upcoming code input directly with “one-click com -
pletion”, thus greatly enhancing coding efficiency. aiXcoder can intelligently search
and recommend standard code for functions similar to the current program during
programming, providing strong reference for programmers.

these models are designed to support. These downstream tasks show how code LLM capabilities
are applied in practice, from generating code from natural language to summarizing, translating,

Mapping downstream code tasks
According to the definition of software engineering, downstream tasks of code can be classified
based on the input-output patterns of code into five types: text-to-code, code-to-code, code-to-
text, code-to-pattern, and text-to-text. The application of LLMs in programming has expanded
from simple single-step tasks, such as code generation and completion, to more complex scenarios
that combine retrieval, repair, testing, reasoning, and cross-file context understanding. In practice,
exploration of some deep domain features often involves combining different downstream tasks
of code, ultimately forming scenarios that better fit business needs, as shown in Figure 9.2.
Figure 9.2: Usage scenarios of code processing tools
The aiXcoder R&D team originates from the Key Laboratory of High Confidence
Software Technologies (Peking University), and it is the first Chinese intelligent
programming assistant based on deep learning code generation technology. As of
March 22, 2022, aiXcoder’s community edition has developer users in more than 130
countries and regions, providing intelligent programming services to over 300,000
international developers. In addition, aiXcoder has launched versions for Android,

52235.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52235.heading: Chapter 9 313
52235.content:
Chapter 9 313
The first category begins with tasks where natural language is used to retrieve, generate, or guide
the creation of code.
Text-to-code tasks
Text-to-code tasks take text as input and output code, typically involving scenarios such as code
retrieval, code generation, and numeric programming:
• Code Retrieval: Aims to search for relevant code based on natural language, or to mine
parallel text-code pairs from unannotated corpora. This task is usually accomplished
by computing the similarity between the query and candidate code embeddings, and
contextual embeddings produced by bidirectional language models (such as BERT) have
been proven to be very useful.
• Code Generation: Aims to generate code based on natural language descriptions, typically
functions or methods. This task can be seen as an upgraded version of code retrieval,
utilizing generative models instead of retrieval models. Statistical Machine Translation
(SMT) and Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models have been widely applied to this
task, often with enhanced decoders utilizing the unique syntactic rules of programming
languages. However, pretrained language models based on the Transformer architecture
have changed this landscape, allowing direct source code generation via autoregressive
language modeling even without task-specific fine-tuning.
• Numeric Programming: Numeric programming is also a special case of code generation,
requiring the language model to solve mathematical reasoning problems by generating
code that will be executed by an external interpreter. This task abstracts the reasoning
process from numerical calculation, so this should be given special consideration when
choosing a code LLM or in practice.
After tasks that generate code from text, the next category focuses on transforming, completing,
repairing, or testing existing code.
Text-to-SQL is a special case of code generation, and this approach is sim -
pler. The model generates SQL commands from natural language queries;
compared to general-purpose languages such as Python and C, SQL has
structured characteristics. Therefore, the text-to-SQL approach has been
widely used in data management.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 314
Code-to-code tasks
Code-to-code tasks take code as input and output code, usually including scenarios such as code
search, code completion, code translation, code repair, and code infilling.
• Code Search: Code search is a task similar to code retrieval. The difference is that the
input consists of existing code fragments, and the programming language used is usually
different from the target language.
• Code Completion: Code completion aims to complete a segment of code based on a given
code prefix. This essentially applies language modeling to code, and related technologies

52236.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52236.heading: Chapter 9 313
52236.content:
such as N-gram, RNN, and Transformer have gradually been introduced. However, due to
the structured nature of programming languages, many early studies found that syntax-
assisted statistical models performed better, and neural models only became mainstream
after 2018.
• Code Translation: The goal of code translation is to translate a segment of code (usually a
function or method) into another programming language. The relationship between code
translation and cross-language code search is similar to that between code generation and
text-to-code retrieval, and SMT/MNT models are also widely applied to this task. Code
generation can help programmers write code snippets, but code translation is different;
it is an important technology for migrating old projects written in outdated languages.
However, we have not yet seen such applications, because even for such projects, the
context window of the most powerful language models is still quite limited.
• Code Repair: Code repair, also known as bug fixing, aims to fix erroneous code. Like code
translation, it is also a traditional code-to-code task, with Cloze tests as a typical example.
Cloze tests are code processing tasks proposed after the rise of BERT-style pre-training.
Owing to the specific semantics of programming languages, this test usually selects several
keywords such as min and max.
• Code Infilling: Code infilling is another task put forward after the popularity of
intermediate infilling pre-training. It is a scenario of code completion, where not only
the left context is given, but also the right context. However, it differs from the Cloze test
in that the Cloze test targets only a single token, while code infilling can target entire
lines or even multiple lines, which requires the decoder to generate them automatically.
• Unit Test Generation: The purpose of unit test generation is to generate unit tests for a
given program. Before the emergence of Codex and other code LLMs, almost all work in
this field used non-neural approaches. However, in the era of LLMs, this task is becoming
increasingly important. Research shows that the current unit tests used to evaluate the
program generation capabilities of code LLMs may not be sufficient.

52237.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52237.heading: Chapter 9 315
52237.content:
Chapter 9 315
• Assertion Generation: Assertion generation is a task closely related to unit testing. Given a
program and a set of unit tests, the goal of this task is to generate assertions (also known
as oracles in software engineering) so that the program can be evaluated using the unit
tests. This task is not typically the focus of the NLP community, as program generation
tasks for LLM evaluation generally involve independent, competitive approaches, where
simply asserting that the program output matches the expected answer suffices.
• Mutation Generation: The purpose of mutation generation is to produce mutants of
a given program for mutation testing, which is closely related to unit test generation
and assertion generation. Mutants that are not detected by a given set of unit tests and
assertions indicate the need for additional test cases or better assertions. Masking tokens
in the source code and sampling from the output of masked language models has become
a common approach for this task.
• Fuzz Testing: Fuzz testing aims to mutate a given set of unit tests to generate new test cases
and is another task related to software testing. While much of the fuzzing work targets
deep learning libraries, very few have utilized language models to carry out this process.
• Type Prediction: Aims to predict types in dynamic programming languages such as Python
and JavaScript. It has been used as a pre-training objective for code LLMs and is often
simplified to a binary tagging task to predict which tokens in the code are identifiers.
Some downstream tasks move in the opposite direction, using code as the input and producing
natural language descriptions, reviews, or labels.
Code-to-text tasks
Code-to-text tasks take code as input and output text, typically including scenarios such as code
summarization, code review, and identifier prediction.
• Code Summarization: Code summarization, also known as docstring generation, aims
to generate a natural language description for a given piece of code (usually a function
or method). This is the exact opposite of code generation, and SMT/NMT techniques
are also applied here.
• Code Review: Code review aims to automate the process of peer code reviews, and it comes
in various forms. Many early studies formulated it as a binary classification task to accept
or reject modifications upon submission, while other studies used information retrieval
techniques to recommend comments from existing comment repositories. However, as
generative models have become more powerful, researchers have also explored directly
generating review comments as a sequence-to-sequence learning task.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 316
• Identifier Prediction: This is the task of predicting the names of identifiers in the code.
Since these names are believed to contain important semantic information, this task has

52238.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52238.heading: Chapter 9 315
52238.content:
been used for code summarization as well as for the pre-training of code models.
Beyond generating or describing code, code LLMs can also help identify patterns, similarities,
and reasoning structures within code.
Code-to-pattern tasks
Code-to-pattern tasks involve classifying code, typically including scenarios such as clone
detection and code reasoning.
• Clone Detection: This predicts whether two pieces of code are clones of each other. In
software engineering, there are four types of code clones, with the most difficult to identify
being semantic clones —code with different syntax but identical functionality. As this
task can be framed as a sentence pair classification problem, BERT-style language models
have been widely used in this area.
• Code Reasoning: This is a recently introduced downstream code task. This task requires
the model to perform reasoning on code or algorithms and answer related questions
presented in multiple-choice form. The questions may cover areas such as conceptual
understanding, numerical computation, and complexity analysis.
Finally, some programming-related tasks operate mainly on technical text rather than source
code itself.
Text-to-text tasks
Text-to-text tasks take text as input and output text, typically including scenarios such as
document translation and log parsing.
• Document Translation: This refers to the automatic translation of code-related
documentation. Since models, datasets, and prompt strategies for machine translation are
very rich in NLP, the technical implementation of document translation is not complicated.
• Log Parsing: This aims to analyze system logs generated by software products, such as
parsing logs into structured templates or detecting anomalies from raw logs.
After mapping the main downstream code tasks, it is useful to focus on one of the most important
and widely used areas: code generation and completion. Understanding how these technologies
developed helps explain why modern code LLMs are able to move beyond simple token suggestions
toward context-aware code assistance, functional code generation, and project-level development
support.

52239.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52239.heading: Chapter 9 317
52239.content:
Chapter 9 317
Tracing the evolution of code generation and
completion
Code programming assistance technologies have a history of more than 40 years. Their
development has gone through several stages, from syntax highlighting, integration within
integrated development environments (IDEs), to code analysis and specification checks.
Among these, tools such as IDEs have been iconic over the past 20 years. They significantly
improve development efficiency and quality through features like automatic code completion,
code highlighting, syntax error prompts, and code snippets, while also delivering a superior
programming experience to developers.
LLM technologies have achieved remarkable breakthroughs and success in general industries,
especially excelling in natural language processing tasks. General-purpose LLMs typically possess
some programming capabilities. However, since their training data mainly consists of general
natural language texts—while programming languages are more structured, have explicit
syntax rules, and more direct and precise semantics—their performance in code understanding
and generation, which is a specialized field, may be limited to some extent. This characteristic
distinguishes them from general-purpose large models.
To better meet developers’ needs in code-related tasks, LLMs are trained on large-scale code
repositories, learning code snippets, programming patterns, and coding conventions, thus better
understanding code structure and logic and generating code that adheres to syntax and semantic
requirements.
In practice, how to effectively improve the efficiency and quality of software development has
always been a concern in the field of software engineering. Among various approaches, code
generation, and completion technologies are considered important methods for enhancing
software development automation and ensuring quality, attracting widespread attention from
both academia and industry. Code generation and completion refers to using certain techniques
to automatically generate source code for software, aiming to enable automatic programming
based on user requirements. This greatly reduces developers’ development burden and allows
them to focus more on delivering business value.
In academia, code generation and completion is an important branch of program synthesis,
aiming to assist, or even replace, programmers in writing code. Automatic generation of front-end
code is divided into two approaches: view code and logic code. Common solutions for generating
view code include automatic generation from design drafts, such as imgcook. Common schemes
for generating logic code include visual orchestration-based generation, input-output sample-
based generation, code corpus-based generation, and function description-based generation.

52240.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52240.heading: Chapter 9 317
52240.content:
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 318
Common code generation and completion techniques
Code generation and completion techniques belong to program automation technology and are
also an important component of modern integrated development environments. Code completion
greatly improves programming efficiency and reduces spelling errors during the coding process.
Code generation and completion techniques typically help programmers predict class names,
method names, keywords, and so on. The prediction of the next token is the most common
form in code generation and completion processes, and is also the mainstream method used by
current IDEs. In common IDEs, the recommended tokens are often listed in alphabetical order,
which increases the time it takes for programmers to select a candidate token, often leading to
a suboptimal user experience.
Traditional code generation and completion approaches are mainly divided into two types. One
type utilizes static type information combined with various heuristic rules to decide which token
to predict, such as method names, parameters, etc. This method rarely considers the semantic
information from code context; for example, the mainstream code completion system in Eclipse
uses static category information to recommend Java methods to users, and the recommended
method names are usually sorted alphabetically. The other method leverages code samples
and previous semantic context to complete code. In 2009, Bruch et al., in the paper Learning
from Examples to Improve Code Completion Systems, described the use of the kNN (k-Nearest
Neighbor) algorithm to match the current completion semantics with previous code samples,
thereby improving completion accuracy. Techniques that use preceding semantic context for code
completion usually utilize special types of context information (such as the set of APIs being called)
to assist with completion. In 2010, Huo et al., in the paper Towards a better code completion system by
API grouping, filtering, and popularity-based ranking, proposed a code completion technique called
BCC. This technique implements Eclipse’s type-based code completion system by ranking and
filtering APIs. This approach usually requires manually defining many heuristic rules to specify
the set of contextual semantics, and if the semantic context at the current completion position
does not match the defined set, this method will fail.
Deep learning methods improve the accuracy of token recommendation by learning the probability
distribution among code tokens from large-scale codebases. The first proposal for probabilistic
modeling of code token sequences was presented by Hindle et al. in their 2012 paper On the
Naturalness of Software. Theoretically, programming languages are written by humans, exhibiting

52241.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52241.heading: Chapter 9 317
52241.content:
repetitive language patterns. Thus, they possess some predictable statistical features that can
be captured by language models. This hypothesis has become the cornerstone for applying
probabilistic models and even deep learning to learn programming languages.

52242.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52242.heading: Chapter 9 319
52242.content:
Chapter 9 319
The most direct approach to next-token prediction is to use the program’s token sequence to
predict the current completion position, employing deep learning to accomplish code completion
as shown in Figure 9.3. This process mainly consists of two parts: the training phase and the code
generation and completion phase.
Figure 9.3: The workflow of code completion using deep learning
Researchers first collect a large amount of data from open-source code repositories or open-
source communities to serve as the corpus for deep learning. To learn from the code in the corpus
more effectively, researchers typically process the source code using code parsers, for example,
converting source code into token sequences or abstract syntax trees. Subsequently, researchers
select or design a deep neural network suitable for their specific task and train it using the data
from the corpus. Currently, the deep neural networks frequently used in code completion tasks
are language models; for example, recurrent neural networks can effectively learn the sequence
characteristics of programs and apply these features to code completion tasks. During the code
generation and completion phase, a partial code snippet is input, and the trained deep learning
model is invoked at the current completion point.
Code generation and completion technologies have developed through several technical paths,
each using a different kind of input, structure, or model to help produce code.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 320
Code generation and completion based on visual orchestration
Visual programming is not a new concept. From the earliest visual plugins to today’s low-code
and no-code technologies, all fall within the realm of visual programming. Visual programming
uses some componentized integrated code visualization platforms to allow so-called “junior
developers” who lack professional coding skills and development experience to independently
organize or participate in application development. In this way, code development expands
from a programmer-exclusive duty to a wider audience. It mainly allows programmers to use
various controls provided by the software itself to build various interfaces of applications in a
modular, building-block-like fashion. Visual orchestration is better suited for the generation of
interface view code.
Currently, there are many platforms that enable visual programming and low-code programming.
Typical representatives include OutSystems, Mendix, Salesforce, and Younuo Technology.
Similarly, there are also many visual solutions for relevant logic code: some are realized through
visual plugins, some through visual components, and others via low-code technologies.
Apart from business scenarios, some emerging fields also adopt visual coding as a business model,

such as simple logic programming for children. For enterprises, with market changes, business
logic, and system architecture are increasingly complex; personnel involved in related businesses
also need to possess a certain degree of reverse engineering thinking skills. Therefore, replacing
programming languages with graphical methods can improve the involvement of business
personnel in the software delivery process.
The advantage of current mainstream logical code visual orchestration solutions lies in highlighting
visual flow and the efficiency brought about by reusable logic nodes. The core is to break down
complex business processes, incorporating input/output and logic processing details into the
specific form rules of each business node. Figure 9.4 shows a complete logical orchestration process.

Among them, node materials are used to define elements in the editor, including icons in the
toolbox, ports, and component schemas in the properties panel. The logic orchestration editor
is a visual editor that, based on the component information provided by the materials, edits and
produces JSON-formatted orchestration description data. The orchestration description data is
the output of user operations in the editor and is consumed by the parsing engine. The front-end
parsing engine, implemented in TypeScript, directly parses the “orchestration description data”
and executes it, thereby realizing the business logic of the software. The back-end parsing engine
can also directly parse and execute the “orchestration description data,” thus implementing the
business logic of the software.
Visual orchestration is suitable for scenarios with a high degree of logic reuse. The reusable
logic can be abstracted as nodes. The granularity of node reuse is crucial. If the granularity is as
large as a functional service, it can be considered business process orchestration. Scenarios with
high business process reuse are suitable for business parties to operate directly through visual
orchestration tools. If the granularity is as small as the expression level, it can be considered
business logic orchestration. A granularity that is too fine requires users to have a programming
mindset; in such cases, users with programming skills can achieve higher efficiency by writing
code directly.
While visual orchestration relies on reusable nodes and predefined flows, programming by
examples allows users to describe desired behavior through sample inputs and outputs.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 322
Code generation and completion based on input–output
examples
Automatically inferring and generating logic programs based on input-output examples is called
PBE (Programming by Examples). PBE is a subfield of program synthesis. The paper Program
Synthesis Using Natural Language proposed a technical solution for program generation. In practical
applications, there is an intuitive and easy-to-implement case of program generation, namely the
Auto-fill function in Excel. This function can quickly generate formulas for table items based on
several examples. For instance, in Figure 9.5, the values 2 and 4 in the first column can be used to
fill in even numbers, and the values 50 and 40 in the second column can automatically deduce
the result of an arithmetic sequence formula.

Another path is to generate or complete code by learning from existing code corpora, where
repositories and snippets become reusable sources of programming knowledge.
Code generation and completion based on code corpora
The prerequisite for code generation and completion based on a code corpus is having a sufficient
corpus, which we often refer to as code snippets. Traditional IDE plugins have already initially
implemented the collection and analysis of common code snippets, which is a relatively common
way of analyzing a code corpus. With the development of code repository technology, analyzing
and utilizing the large amount of code accumulated in repositories to eventually form a company’s
core assets—transforming the value of code into proprietary technology and intellectual property—
has become a new direction for technological output. At the same time, combining code corpus
with management measures and deeply embedding code LLM technology into development and
management processes to form domain knowledge and management standards has become an
ongoing research topic for many enterprises, as shown in Figure 9.8.

fixed corpora, users preset code snippets, which are then prompted to the user by listening to
shortcut keys entered by the user to search for the corresponding snippet. This code generation
method is simple and fast, but it suffers from poor scalability and suboptimal user experience,
and developers need to know the key values and corresponding snippets in advance.
The acquisition of intelligent corpora mainly depends on the capability of the code repository
itself and the assistance of models. Typical examples include the GitHub Copilot plugin and
N-gram models. The VSCode plugin Kite Autocomplete uses the N-gram model and is trained
on over 25 million files, enhancing coding efficiency through code assistance functions during
programming. It predicts the content that the user is about to input based on context and current
input. Additionally, it can read ahead in the context of the entire file to further infer the user’s

Instead of starting from existing code snippets, functional-description-based methods begin

Code generation and completion based on functional
descriptions
We often use natural language to describe program functionality, and generating programs
automatically from natural language descriptions is extremely challenging. The diversity of
natural language texts and programs, the ambiguity of text, and the complex structure of code
make establishing the connection between text and code a difficult problem. In this section, we
describe how code generation and completion can be performed based on functional descriptions
using the tools NL2SQL and NL2IFTTT.

52248.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52248.heading: NL2SQL
52248.content:
NL2SQL
NL2SQL (Natural Language to SQL) is a cutting-edge research direction in conversational user
interfaces (Conversation User Interface, CUI), aiming to convert user input in natural language
into executable SQL statements, thereby improving the efficiency of user data queries. Currently,
the main challenge hindering the value realization of big data is the high threshold for data access,
relying on database administrators to write complex SQL statements, and the added complexity
and diversity of Chinese expressions. There is substantial research in this field both domestically
and abroad, with most of the well-known NL2SQL datasets being in English, such as WikiSQL,
Spider, CoSQL, etc.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 328
A typical three-layer architecture of NL2SQL is shown in Figure 9.11.
Figure 9.11: Typical three-layer architecture of NL2SQL
NL2SQL consists of a user interaction page, a processing unit, and a database. The processing
unit is the core of the entire architecture, responsible for semantic parsing and connecting the
interaction channel between the user and the system, encompassing key technologies such as
intelligent word segmentation, entity recognition, and knowledge retrieval. In the research
direction of converting natural language into executable SQL statements, the internal algorithms
of the processing unit are gradually evolving toward deep learning.
In the Chinese NL2SQL competition, the research team from the National University of Defense
Technology proposed the M-SQL model, which achieved 92% accuracy on Chinese datasets. In
addition, running one epoch of the M-SQL model on a single 2080Ti GPU takes 20 minutes, and
the model only needs 3–4 epochs to converge.
Unlike the M-SQL model from the National University of Defense Technology, Google’s Analyza
uses a semantic parsing and rule-based approach, which offers strong controllability but requires
manual maintenance of rules. Analyza implements NL2SQL through deep learning using an
encoder-decoder architecture, recognizing several SQL clauses, including SELECT and WHERE
clauses, and sometimes involving operators such as GROUP BY and LIMIT. Each part involves
many details, such as table recognition, attribute recognition, etc. Different algorithms make
improvements and optimizations on these details within this framework to achieve better results.

52249.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52249.heading: Chapter 9 329
52249.content:
Chapter 9 329
Although end-to-end NL2SQL solutions can reduce manual maintenance costs, they perform
well only in simple scenarios like WikiSQL. For more complex scenarios, such as Spider or CoSQL,
accuracy is relatively low, and it is difficult to meet commercial application requirements.

52250.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52250.heading: NL2IFTTT
52250.content:
NL2IFTTT
IFTTT stands for ‘ if this then that ’. It is an innovative platform service that determines whether
to execute the next command based on conditions from different platforms. For example, when
someone in an IM marks a photo containing you, the photo can automatically be backed up to
your phone’s photo album. This approach meets the user’s need to link content from service A
to service B, without requiring manual intervention—the related action can be initiated and
completed automatically by IFTTT.
NL2IFTTT generates IFTTT code through natural language. Compared to commonly used
programming languages, its structure is more concise and easier to learn in terms of its structural
rules. IFTTT is based on task-triggered conditions, similar to a simplified programming language,
that is, ‘if behavior B of event A occurs, then execute C.’
Language-model-based approaches extend these earlier methods by learning statistical and
semantic patterns from large collections of code, enabling more flexible prediction, completion,
and generation.
Code generation and completion based on language models
Language models are widely used in various natural language processing tasks, such as machine
translation, speech recognition, question answering systems, etc. Language models define
the probability distribution of token sequences in natural language. Due to the naturalness
of programming languages, language models are also applied to program modeling, usually
by directly inputting parsed code snippets (at the word or character level) as text. The goal of
this model is to model the textual probability distribution of programming languages, i.e., the
probabilistic model is used to estimate the probability distribution P (s) of a code snippet s. For
a code snippet s = { w 1, …, w m }, the language model calculates the probability distribution of the
entire code snippet by computing the conditional probability of each word based on the previously
generated words, i.e.,
NL2IFTTT is included here as a case study in DSL-targeted code generation rather
than as a representative of mainstream NL-to-code research.

52251.heading: NL2IFTTT
52251.content:
Naturalness of Software, many works utilizing N-gram models emerged subsequently. Although
N-gram can effectively learn the local context of code snippets, it cannot understand the semantic
information of code snippets. To address this problem, many researchers have improved the
N-gram model by combining the characteristics of software engineering tasks. Nguyen et al., in
the paper A Statistical Semantic Language Model for Source Code, proposed the idea that the SLAMC
model incorporates global information into the N-gram model; SLAMC combines semantic
information and models rules for semantic annotations. This method achieved a significant
improvement in the accuracy of code recommendation compared to a regular N-gram. Meanwhile,
Raychev et al., in the paper Code Completion with Statistical Language Models, also proposed
combining the N-gram model with RNN, actively suggesting appropriate API calls based on the
context during Java development to implement code completion. To address the challenge of the
locality property of code, Tu et al. proposed in the paper On the Localness of Software to introduce
a caching mechanism into the N-gram model, utilizing the characteristic that identifiers tend to
repeatedly appear within a close range, thereby achieving significant results in code prediction.
Compared to N-gram, RNN can not only capture regularities among words in a sentence, but
also detect relationships between more distant words. To further address the long-distance
dependency problem, many RNN-based variants, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and
Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), have been proposed and widely applied. As shown in Figure 9.12,
RNN models can effectively model source code and learn vector representations of source code.

52252.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52252.heading: Chapter 9 331
52252.content:
Chapter 9 331
Figure 9.12: Modeling process of RNN model
The paper DeepAM-Migrate APIs with Multi-Modal Sequence to Sequence Learning focuses on using
RNN to learn vector representations that differentiate Java and C# API, and applies these learned
vectors to the API migration task between these two languages to generate code at the API level.
Many researchers have used RNN models for code token prediction and completion, achieving
remarkable results. Most research models code at the word level using RNNs, but due to the large
number of variables in code, learning becomes very challenging; therefore, some work has started
to model code at the character level.
Programming languages exhibit certain local repetitiveness. For example, a defined variable is
often reused later in the code. However, these variables are largely treated as out-of-vocabulary
(OoV) words, usually represented as UNK. Predicting a UNK is of no help to programmers in their
coding, so researchers have considered incorporating pointer network mechanisms into language
models to accurately predict locally repeated words. The pointer network can effectively copy
words that need to be reused from the input code snippet. Pointer networks were first proposed at
the 2015 IEEE conference, originally used to solve combinatorial optimization problems, and are
a variant of neural machine translation models (i.e., sequence-to-sequence models, Seq2Seq
models). In pointer networks, the attention mechanism is simpler, as it does not consider the
input elements, but instead points to them probabilistically.
In 2016, Bhoopchand et al. proposed a Sparse Pointer Network in the paper Learning Python Code
Suggestion with a Sparse Pointer Network, mainly addressing the issue of predicting custom identifiers
(such as class names, method names, variable names, etc.). The paper defines the concept of
“memory” to store the previous K identifiers. The method maintains a vector m=[id1,...,id*K*],
used to record the positions of identifiers in the global vocabulary, i.e., pointers to the global
vocabulary.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 332
At each prediction step, the network combines the global language model distribution, the pointer
probability distribution over custom identifiers, and the current code input to determine the output
word. Compared to traditional recurrent neural networks (without the attention mechanism),
this method increases the accuracy for predicting custom Python identifiers by about 25%.
In their 2018 paper Code Completion with Neural Attention and Pointer Networks, Li et al. proposed
a method for code completion by combining a language model with an attention mechanism
and pointer networks, modeling sequences of abstract syntax trees (ASTs). This model can not
only predict the type of AST nodes but also predict their values, that is, the code to be completed.

52253.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52253.heading: Chapter 9 331
52253.content:
When predicting code, the entropy of parent nodes is greater than that of child nodes, resulting
in higher prediction accuracy. Therefore, their attention mechanism incorporates the parent-
child node relationship of syntax trees into the traditional attention mechanism. The paper uses
pointer networks to copy words from the input code snippets to predict OoV tokens. By defining
a selector, the model decides whether to predict the next word based on the distribution over
the global vocabulary in the language model or to use the pointer network to copy a word from
the input code snippet. This method was validated on both Python and JavaScript datasets, and
results show that the method performs exceptionally well in OoV prediction scenarios.
Although code generation and completion technologies have advanced significantly, they still
face practical limitations when applied to real software projects. The next section examines the
main issues that affect their reliability, adaptability, and usefulness in production development
environments.
Identifying pain points in code generation and
completion
Overall, code generation and completion based on LLM technology has become a trend, but the
application of this technology is still at an early stage, mainly facing the following pain points.
Uneven quality of training corpora
In daily work, the corpora used to train models can be roughly divided into two categories: one
consists of programs constructed artificially based on DSL technology, and the other consists of
project programs crawled from open source communities. Programs based on DSL usually have
relatively simple syntax and short length, making them easy to train and test; however, models
designed for DSL are difficult to generalize to other languages. Project programs crawled from
open source communities are closer to actual software development, but it is difficult to guarantee
the quality of the code.

52254.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52254.heading: Chapter 9 333
52254.content:
Chapter 9 333
Low-quality, non-standard code introduces additional noise risk to neural networks, and code
that uses different programming conventions causes confusion for neural network models during
training and prediction. Therefore, how to obtain a unified, standardized, high-quality program
corpus is a challenge.
Weak generalization ability of program code
Much program code consists of business domain-specific logic, requiring a substantial amount
of domain-specific logic resources and a deep understanding of the various services relied on by
existing businesses. New businesses need to train their own models based on their own material
libraries, and the services required by completely new businesses often need to be developed
from scratch. Supplying new materials can also be difficult, unless all the dependent services are
indivisible atomic services; thus, making the logic model universal is hard to achieve.
Information asymmetry between functional descriptions and
program code
In actual project development, it is common for requirement descriptions to be more advanced
and abstract than functional descriptions. Requirement descriptions must first be converted
into functional descriptions, then into code descriptions, and finally, program code is generated.
At each stage, there will be information loss, which is currently typically compensated for by
programmers’ business knowledge and programming experience. There are three solutions for
directly generating code from functional descriptions:
• End-to-end generation of abstract syntax trees from requirement descriptions. If the
product definition’s description of software functionality is precise enough, this is
equivalent to creating a higher-level descriptive language
• Abstracting and encapsulating the entire chain from functional description to code as
a larger-grain functional description. Most encapsulation-based methods are currently
feasible and effective, with a typical example being NL2IFTTT.
• Developers deeply engage in each business domain, and at each stage, from functional
description to code, the model understands layer by layer and gradually generates the code
Therefore, the quality of the corpus and the accuracy of the model are crucial.
The limitations of code generation and completion become more pronounced when models are
asked to work across real project repositories rather than isolated functions or snippets. This is
where agent-based methods become important: they combine code LLMs with tools, execution
environments, documentation, and iterative feedback to support more complex project-level
development tasks.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 334
Applying agent-based methods to project-level code
generation
Agent-based project-level code generation extends single-function code completion by combining

52255.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52255.heading: Chapter 9 333
52255.content:
a code LLM with tools — a code execution sandbox, a static analyzer, a documentation lookup
— orchestrated by an LLM agent that plans, calls tools, and iterates. The Xcoder team at Peking
University has achieved significant results in research on the application of code LLM-based
agents in the field of software engineering, publishing several relevant papers. Xcoder is an early
example of a code LLM-based agent system that combines a code-focused language model with
tools to address project-level code generation problems. This section uses Peking University’s
paper CODEAGENT—Enhancing Code Generation with Tool-Integrated Agent Systems for Real-World
Repo-level Coding Challenges to explain Agent-based project-level code generation methods.
Pain points of project-level code generation in enterprises
Project-level code in enterprises, as a critical component supporting and driving the core business
processes, is directly related to the quality of the enterprise’s products and services, operational
efficiency, and market competitiveness. However, project-level code often involves diverse library
and function calls, complex contextual dependencies across the codebase, and various types of
code documentation. Furthermore, as business requirements change, the project code needs
constant updating, expansion, and optimization. In this dynamic, ongoing, and complex process,
there are numerous pain points.
Difficulty in fine-grained code modification and expansion
A project usually contains thousands or even tens of thousands of lines of code, involving multiple
interdependent modules and subsystems. When faced with the need for fine-grained code changes,
even a “single move can affect the whole picture”; a slight mishap can impact other modules,
leading to extensive testing and verification work. This further affects project schedules and
increases the complexity and risks of maintenance.
Complex and large codebases
Large-scale projects generally have long cycles and high staff turnover. The complexity and
vastness of the codebase make it difficult for new team members to quickly grasp the project
structure and code logic; even experienced members face time-consuming and labor-intensive
efforts when searching for specific code fragments in the ever-growing codebase.

52256.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52256.heading: Chapter 9 335
52256.content:
Chapter 9 335
Difficulty ensuring code generation quality
In actual programming, developers commonly use various tools to assist with coding, such as
search engines, documentation readers, and code testing tools. Although code LLMs possess
powerful code generation capabilities, they lack the ability to interact with these tools, which
limits their performance in complex tasks. Moreover, due to issues such as hallucinations with
code LLMs, the generated code may use incorrect APIs, making it difficult to ensure the quality
and reliability of code generation.
Low efficiency in implementing requirements into code
Throughout the entire project development process, enterprises often face issues such as
insufficient requirement understanding, frequent architecture design adjustments, difficulty
controlling development progress, and inadequate test coverage. These result in low iteration
efficiency, project delays, budget overruns, or substandard quality, further increasing operational
burdens and impacting market competitiveness.
Facing numerous pain points and challenges in project-level code generation, introducing
Agents has become a key path for enterprises to resolve difficulties in code generation, improve
development efficiency and code quality, and accelerate product iteration.
Technical implementation of agents
The technical implementation of a code agent can be understood from two related perspectives:
how the agent is evaluated in realistic repository-level tasks, and how the agent uses tools to
navigate code, gather context, generate implementations, and test the results. The following
discussion first examines the testing process used to evaluate Code Agent, then explains the
framework and tool integration that support project-level code generation.
Code agent testing process
The Xcoder team at Peking University conducted extensive testing on the Code Agent. Since
enterprises mainly use open-source codebases in actual coding processes—and codebases contain
a large number of complex code invocation relationships—testing within a codebase is the only
way to obtain precise results, enabling the code LLM agent to function properly. To this end,
the team configured corresponding corpora for each test task, including documentation, code
dependencies, and runtime environment.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 336
Documentation is the main input for testing and mainly describes the target for corpus generation.
The documentation provides information beyond natural language requirements, including class-
level (class names, signatures, and member functions) and function-level (function descriptions
and parameter descriptions) information. Generally, the correctness of programs generated by the
Agent can be verified by testing tools. The generated program must meet interface requirements

52257.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52257.heading: Chapter 9 335
52257.content:
(e.g., input parameters), so the documentation under test also provides the type and explanation
for input parameters and output values. Considering that requirements often involve terms specific
to certain domains, the documentation also explains these terms, such as certain mathematical
formulas. Related test information is shown in Figure 9.13.
Figure 9.13: Test information for generated programs
The team specifically tested for context dependencies, which is a distinct feature from the
experiments of others. From the perspective of code generation and completion, this testing detail
is especially important because, in actual applications, a class or function usually interacts with
other code fragments in the same codebase. Such situations often occur in import statements
or within the same project, where user-defined code also depends on other user-defined code.
The interactions and dependencies among these codes can happen within the same file or span
multiple files.

52258.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52258.heading: Chapter 9 337
52258.content:
Chapter 9 337
For example, implementing the RandomForest class in Figure 9.14 depends on the boot-strap_
sample function in rf.py and the DecisionTree class in dt.py. This is a case of complex code
context dependency.
Figure 9.14: Contextual dependency of code
During the testing process, the tool designed by the Xcoder team at Peking University extracts
all user-defined elements (such as class names, function names, constants, and global variables)
as well as public library names from each file and stores these elements in a knowledge base. For
any defined function, the tool can use the knowledge base to locate its source file, parse the file
to identify all user-defined symbols and public libraries, and finally determine their contextual
dependencies through exact matching of symbol names and scopes.

Toward a Unified Agent with Foundation Models, the team proposed a new code-agent framework
based on code LLMs: Code Agent. This framework leverages external tools to enhance the code
LLM’s ability to solve problems in complex repository-level code generation. Whenever tools
are called, the Code Agent seamlessly and automatically generates code and outputs the results
after integration. Code Agent can help code LLMs complete the entire automatic code generation
process, including information gathering, code implementation, and code testing, and interact
better with software coding tools, as shown in Figure 9.15.

Summary
In this chapter, you learned how LLMs are applied in programming scenarios to support code
understanding, code generation, code completion, and project-level development, while also
exploring how agent-based approaches can help teams handle complex enterprise codebases
more efficiently. The chapter also showed how large code models improve developer productivity
across downstream coding tasks and real-world software engineering workflows.
Building on these programming-focused applications, the next chapter shifts to project

Applying LLMs in Project
Management
During the project management process, project managers encounter various issues in the
requirements analysis phase, task planning phase, risk management phase, as well as in the
communication and collaboration phases. These issues become increasingly prominent, especially
in large-scale projects. With technological innovation and development, LLMs have gradually
been applied in project management scenarios. For example, in the requirements analysis phase,
LLMs can help project teams extract key information from various sources, quickly organize
and understand complex requirement statements. When clients express their expectations for a
product in large volumes of natural language, the model can summarize the core requirements
and key points. In the communication and collaboration phase, LLMs can assist project managers
in formulating detailed project plans, including task breakdown, time estimation, and resource
allocation.
This chapter covers the following main topics:
• Analyzing requirements and planning project tasks
• Improving communication and collaboration
• Managing project risks and supporting decisions
• Optimizing project execution with intelligent workflows
• Applying LLMs in project management case studies
Applying LLMs in Project Management 346
Analyzing requirements and planning project tasks
In project management practice, clarifying project requirements is foundational work and the
key to ensuring the smooth execution of subsequent tasks. During the requirements analysis
stage, the project team is expected to accurately capture and analyze user expectations and the
core business objectives to ensure that the project’s final deliverables meet the requirements.
After requirements analysis, the task planning stage transforms these requirements into specific,
actionable steps and activities, which are further detailed with schedules and resource allocations
to ensure each phase is effectively controlled and supervised.
In both of these processes, the collection and processing of a large amount of information, as well

52265.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52265.heading: Chapter 9 343
52265.content:
as complex logical reasoning, are indispensable. Traditional methods often rely on the expertise
of professionals through manual operations, which are less efficient and prone to omissions or
errors due to human factors. With technological advancements, especially the application of AI
technologies such as LLMs, this situation has been significantly improved.
LLMs possess powerful natural language processing capabilities, enabling project teams to
quickly extract key information from a vast number of documents and communications, and to
understand and summarize user requirements and underlying intentions through deep learning
algorithms. In addition, these models can automatically generate requirement documents, provide
task planning suggestions, predict potential issues, and perform risk assessments. Through these
advanced functions, project managers can complete requirements analysis and task planning
more efficiently and accurately, thereby improving project quality and success rates.
The first step in this process is understanding what stakeholders actually need, because unclear
or incomplete requirements can affect every later decision in the project.
Requirements analysis
As a core aspect of project management, requirements analysis plays a critical role that cannot
be overlooked. It determines whether the project can proceed smoothly and ultimately achieve
its intended goals. In traditional project management, requirements analysis is the process of
identifying and understanding what the client or user needs. This step is crucial to ensuring the
ultimate success of the project. Traditional methods of requirements analysis include meetings,
individual interviews, focus groups, surveys, and questionnaires. These methods have many
limitations, as shown in Figure 10.1.

52266.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52266.heading: Chapter 10 347
52266.content:
Chapter 10 347
Figure 10.1: Pain points of requirements analysis
These pain points usually arise because traditional requirements analysis depends heavily on
manual coordination, subjective interpretation, and limited sources of information:
• Traditional requirements analysis is time-consuming and inefficient. Organizing and
conducting physical meetings often requires coordinating the schedules of numerous
participants, which is a complex and time-consuming task in itself. Additionally, the
information collected from meetings may need further organization and analysis before
useful conclusions can be drawn. Moreover, user interviews and questionnaire surveys
typically require significant manpower to carry out—from designing questionnaires to
distributing, collecting, and analyzing the data—each step consumes a great deal of time,
and various unforeseen challenges may arise throughout the process.
• Limited by participants’ experience and cognitive biases. Requirements analysis often
relies on the subjective judgment of professionals, inevitably introducing their cognitive
biases. For example, project managers and analysts may interpret user needs based on
their own experience and preferences, neglecting or misunderstanding the user’s real
intentions and needs. In addition, due to differences in cultural background, language
communication, or personal preferences, users may not express their needs precisely,
which can easily lead to misinterpretations or omissions of information.
Applying LLMs in Project Management 348
• There is a quality balance issue in requirements analysis. In traditional requirements
analysis, obtaining high-quality information often means having less data because in-
depth interviews and thorough meeting discussions require a lot of time and attention,
making it impossible to cover a wide user base within a limited time. Conversely, to pursue
quantity, the depth and accuracy of data may be sacrificed, and balancing these two
aspects is always difficult.
• Additionally, it is difficult to completely avoid the influence of environmental factors
during meeting discussions and user interviews. Many practitioners may be constrained
by social expectations when expressing themselves in public, unwilling to express their
true thoughts candidly, or may change their opinions due to conformity, all of which
impact the authenticity and accuracy of requirements analysis.
However, with rapid advancements in information technology, especially in the field of artificial
intelligence, the rise of LLMs has opened up brand-new possibilities for requirements analysis.
Innovative technologies represented by ChatGPT have been applied, with ChatGPT’s core
advantage lying in its deep understanding and processing capabilities of natural language, giving

it a distinct edge in complex text data analysis. Figure 10.2 presents several key advantages of
LLMs in requirements analysis scenarios.

52268.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops

52268.content:
Chapter 10 349
When applied to requirements analysis, LLMs help address limitations in several practical ways:
• Rapid Processing of Large Amounts of Data: LLMs can efficiently process massive text
datasets, such as lengthy project files, intensive email correspondence, and detailed
meeting minutes. Analyzing this content manually could require significant time and
effort, while LLMs can accomplish the same tasks quickly, saving vast resources.
• Deep Learning and Understanding: Leveraging advanced machine learning algorithms
and extensive training datasets, LLMs can not only identify keywords and phrases in text
but also understand their context and underlying meaning, providing more accurate
information extraction and content analysis.
• Uncovering Implicit Requirements: In traditional requirements analysis, some latent
but unexpressed needs can easily be overlooked. LLMs can use contextual reasoning and
pattern recognition to discover these implicit requirements, helping project teams grasp
a more comprehensive picture of needs.
• Adaptation to Multiple Text Formats: Whether it’s structured reports, unstructured social
media posts, or ad hoc meeting notes, LLMs can comprehend and process different text
formats and extract valid information from these diverse data sources.
• Cross-Domain Knowledge Integration: Cross-domain requirements analysis is often
limited by the analyst’s knowledge scope. Since LLMs are trained on texts covering a wide
range of topics, they possess cross-industry and cross-domain knowledge bases, enabling
them to take richer background knowledge into account and provide comprehensive
insights during analysis.
• Continuous Learning and Improvement: With ongoing input of new data, LLMs can
continue learning and adapting to new linguistic environments and requirement changes,
keeping their analytical abilities up to date.
• Unbiased Objective Analysis: Unlike human analysts who may have cognitive biases,
LLMs can perform unbiased data analysis, objectively distilling information to ensure
the accuracy and fairness of requirements analysis.
• Decision Support: By providing accurate requirements analysis, LLMs can assist managers
and decision-makers in better understanding market and user needs, optimizing the
decision-making process, and thereby improving the success rate and efficiency of projects.
Taken together, these capabilities show that the value of LLMs is not limited to faster text
processing. Their larger contribution lies in helping teams form a clearer, more complete, and
more adaptable understanding of project requirements.
Applying LLMs in Project Management 350
The value proposition of LLMs for requirements analysis
The capabilities of LLMs are reflected not only in rapid processing and in-depth analysis of text
data, but also in their ability to reason over massive amounts of information through continuous

52269.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops

52269.content:
learning. This feature directly addresses the issues raised by Leffingwell in the paper Agile Software
Requirements: Lean Requirements Practices for Teams, Programs, and the Enterprise. With such
advanced analytical power, LLMs can help project teams accurately grasp the complete picture
of requirements at the early stages of a project, thereby preventing or reducing unexpected issues
and resource waste during development.
In addition, LLMs continuously receive new input and use their complex neural network structures
to process this data, allowing them to constantly enhance their insight and become self-optimizing
systems. This enables them to perform excellently in responding to rapidly changing user needs,
discovering, and establishing implicit connections between requirements, and even uncovering
previously unidentified patterns and logical rules. For example, when handling user feedback,
LLMs can not only identify explicit comments, but also reveal subtle shifts in user preferences
and market trends by comparing and associating large amounts of similar data.
Such in-depth mining and intelligent analysis of data improve the team’s grasp of customer
needs. Whether the requirements are straightforward or complex and intertwined, LLMs can
provide all-around support for project teams. This advantage is particularly suitable for projects
involving multi-layered system interactions or those that rapidly evolve with user feedback. In
these cases, the efficient analysis and learning capabilities of LLMs can significantly enhance the
project’s agility and accuracy in responding to the market, helping the project stay on the right
developmental track and reducing uncertainty and risk.
Beyond analyzing and mining requirements, LLMs can also support project teams through
intelligent Q&A and recommendations. They can provide real-time responses based on
queries from project members and offer accurate answers and suggestions to various questions
raised within the team. This instant, targeted interactive approach greatly promotes internal
communication and collaboration within the team and helps ensure that all members have a
unified and accurate understanding of project requirements.
Thus, it can be seen that LLMs have broad application prospects in the field of requirements
analysis. They can not only improve the efficiency and accuracy of analytical work but also increase
the probability of project success and ensure the project continues to advance steadily along the
planned path. As LLM technology continues to improve and become more widespread, it will
inevitably become an indispensable component in the field of project management.

Once requirements are understood and agreed upon, the next step is to convert them into tasks,
timelines, priorities, and resource decisions that the project team can act on.
Task planning
Task planning is also an indispensable aspect of project management, involving key areas such
as task breakdown, prioritization, time scheduling, and resource allocation. Accurate and
efficient task planning ensures smooth project workflows and the achievement of objectives. In
today’s era of big data and artificial intelligence, the application of LLMs provides project teams
with unprecedented support and assistance, greatly enhancing the intelligence of task planning.
By leveraging natural language processing and machine learning technologies, LLMs are able to
deeply analyze massive amounts of historical project data to identify best practices and patterns
of potential failure. Based on the experience of past successful cases, these models can offer
recommendations for current projects, such as which tasks should be prioritized, the expected
timeframe, and how to rationally allocate resources. Additionally, the models can provide
personalized task allocation plans by taking into account the professional expertise and historical
performance of individual team members.
LLMs also possess predictive capabilities for challenges and risks that may be encountered.
By analyzing the incidence rate of issues at similar stages in past projects, combined with the
specific conditions of the current project, the models can foresee and provide early warnings for
potential difficulties and bottlenecks, enabling project managers to proactively take measures
to avoid or mitigate risks.
As agile project management methods become more widely adopted, quick iteration and
adaptability have become increasingly important. As shown in Figure 10.3, the combination of
LLMs with agile methodologies can further promote team collaboration and improve response
speed.

Applying LLMs in Project Management 352
The model can analyze the team’s work output and feedback in real time, dynamically adjusting
task plans to ensure tasks are always aligned with project objectives and meet the latest user needs.
It can optimize workflows in real time based on ongoing task performance, increase transparency,
and enhance communication and cooperation efficiency among team members.
LLMs can also provide real-time monitoring of task execution, collect execution data, and analyze
efficiency bottlenecks to uncover potential systemic issues. Through these insights, the model
not only provides guidance to the team during the execution phase but also offers strategic
improvement suggestions for future project planning.
Overall, the application of LLMs in task planning is not just about providing a simple tool, but

represents a completely new way of working and thinking. It transforms data intelligence into
practical wisdom, providing project teams with greater efficiency and quality assurance, ensuring
steady project advancement and successful delivery. By introducing LLMs, the flexibility and
adaptability of agile methods are further enhanced, creating even greater value and possibilities
for project teams. As AI technology continues to advance, we have reason to believe that LLMs
will become a key driving force in the future development of project management.
Once requirements have been clarified and tasks have been planned, the next challenge is ensuring
that the right information reaches the right people at the right time. This makes communication
and collaboration central to whether project plans can be executed effectively.
Improving communication and collaboration
Project management is a key process to ensure that a project is successfully completed on time,
within budget, and in accordance with quality standards. In this process, communication with
team members, stakeholders, and other relevant parties is crucial. Studies have shown that 70% to
90% of the time in project management work is spent on communication activities. This includes
not only routine exchanges such as task assignment, progress updates, and problem-solving, but
also more complex information exchanges, such as requirements negotiation, risk assessment,
and strategy development, as shown in Figure 10.4.
